metadata.note: The Pacific Coast Railway, the 3 ft narrow gauge that ran from the steamer wharf at Port Harford (renamed Port San Luis in 1909) through San Luis Obispo and Santa Maria to Los Olivos, with its predecessor the San Luis Obispo & Santa Maria Valley Railroad drawn as separate features for the years it owned the line. Added 2026-08-26 to fill a hole: nothing on the map served San Luis Obispo before 1937. In 1897 this narrow gauge and Southern Pacific's stub down to Surf (southern_pacific_coast_division.geojson) were the town's two railways. The modern Santa Margarita Ranch excursion line, a separate company that reuses the name, is the last feature.
metadata.source: OpenStreetMap relation 6454615 and surrounding ways tagged old_railway_operator=Pacific Coast Railway, plus relation 6773665 for the Santa Margarita Ranch excursion line, for geometry; Wikipedia 'Pacific Coast Railway', 'San Luis Obispo station' and 'Pacific Coast Railroad (tourist)', and the Monterey County Historical Society's 'Railroads of the Central Coast' for dates.
metadata.geometry_quality: Port Harford - Los Olivos comes out at 75.1 mi traced against a documented system length of about 76 mi, and the Port Harford - San Luis Obispo end at 10.1 mi against a documented 10 mi. 13.6 mi of the total is straight-line bridging where the grade is built over or unmapped; the four legs longer than 1.5 mi are the crossing of San Luis Obispo itself (2.2 mi in and 1.5 mi out, routed via the depot site at Higuera and South streets), 1.9 mi north of Santa Maria, 2.5 mi south of Santa Maria and 3.4 mi over the divide into the Los Alamos valley. Each feature's own geometry_quality names its share. The drawn alignment is the railway's own - the grade was never relocated, only abandoned.
metadata.freight_only_audit: 2026-08-26: the Pacific Coast Railway's branches are deliberately not drawn. The Betteravia branch (1899, electrified 1906, extended to Guadalupe 1909) served the Union Sugar refinery and the Sisquoc branch (1910, electrified) served an oil refinery; both were freight operations, so under Rule 1 they get no drawn years. An 18.8 km abandoned Santa Maria - Sisquoc grade found in OSM during tracing was excluded on those grounds.
metadata.horsecar_audit: 2026-08-26: the 2 ft 6 in horse-powered tramway Ah Louis built between Port Harford and Avila in 1873 is not drawn. Under Rule 5 the Port Harford line starts in 1876, when steam-worked track reached San Luis Obispo. San Luis Obispo's own San Luis Street Railway, running on Higuera Street from about 1890, was horse-drawn and is excluded for the same reason; no evidence was found that it ever electrified.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: The year Pacific Coast Railway passenger or mixed-train service actually ended is not established. The sources give 1930 (Los Olivos cut to a twice-weekly mixed train), 1933 (Los Olivos service ends), 1936 (line beyond Los Alamos dismantled), 1941 (operations end) and 1942 (rails lifted), but none says when the railway stopped carrying people on the surviving Port San Luis - Santa Maria portion. That portion is drawn to 1941, the end of all operations, which may over-assert passenger service in its final years. No milepost table or station list was obtained, so the split points between features are geocoded town centres, not sourced junctions - Arroyo Grande in particular is 1.3 km off the traced line. No timetable was consulted: every headway_min and avg_speed_kmh in this layer is an estimate.

segments.note: The Pacific Coast Steamship Company's 3 ft gauge San Luis Obispo & Santa Maria Valley Railroad, built to feed coastwise steamers at the Port Harford wharf. Steam operation began in 1875 and the track was completed into San Luis Obispo on August 8 1876. A horse-powered 2 ft 6 in tramway had run Port Harford - Avila from 1873; that animal-powered era is deliberately not drawn. Drawn to 1882, when this company merged with the Pacific Coast Railroad Company to form the Pacific Coast Railway - the successor is a separate feature in the new owner's colour.
sources: Segment-level: construction dates from Wikipedia's Pacific Coast Railway article and the Monterey County Historical Society's 'Railroads of the Central Coast'; the headway is an estimate.

segments.note: Under the Pacific Coast Railway, formed by the 1882 merger of the San Luis Obispo & Santa Maria Valley Railroad with the Pacific Coast Railroad Company. Until Southern Pacific came over Cuesta Pass in May 1894, this narrow gauge and the steamers waiting at Port Harford were San Luis Obispo's only common-carrier link to the world.

segments.note: Peak years, feeding Southern Pacific's through Coast Line trains at San Luis Obispo from 1901 as well as the steamers. Over 62,000 passenger fares were collected in 1912, the railway's best year. Port Harford was renamed Port San Luis in 1909. headway_min is an estimate.

segments.note: Arroyo Grande was reached in 1881 and Santa Maria in 1882, the year the Pacific Coast Railway was formed, so the new company worked the whole of this stretch from the start. Through the 1890s it was the only rail service down the Arroyo Grande and Santa Maria valleys, and from 1895 it faced Southern Pacific's new standard gauge on a roughly parallel alignment.

properties.speed_source: Estimate. A ranch excursion line runs at walking-to-jogging pace; no published figure was consulted.

segments.note: A modern 3 ft gauge heritage operation at Santa Margarita Ranch, north of San Luis Obispo over Cuesta Pass, established in 2000 and completed in 2004. It carries passengers on limited public excursions, so it counts as passenger service and is drawn as tourist_rail. It is unrelated corporately to the historical Pacific Coast Railway whose name it echoes, hence the separate company and colour. headway_min is a placeholder - operation is occasional, not scheduled.
sources: Segment-level: 2000 establishment and 2004 completion from Wikipedia's Pacific Coast Railroad (tourist) article; the operating frequency is not sourced.
